Oaf7e7.title: We take them for granted, but where would we be without them? Antibiotics: the backbone of modern medicine
Oaf7e7.text:
Antibiotics are one of the foundations of modern healthcare. They treat serious bacterial infections and make many of the treatments we now take for granted, from major surgery to cancer treatment, much safer.
This World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week (18–24 November), Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex, explains why we all have a role in protecting antibiotics for the future.
Imagine breaking your leg badly, with an open wound that becomes infected. Today, doctors can treat that infection with antibiotics. Now imagine that the bacteria causing the infection are resistant to the antibiotics we have available. Suddenly, something we would normally expect to treat can become much more dangerous. That isn’t science fiction. Antibiotics continue to save lives every day, but antibiotic-resistant infections are already happening and are becoming an increasing threat.
Help keep antibiotics working
Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections and are also essential to much of modern medicine, including surgery and the treatment of serious wounds. But every time we use an antibiotic there is an opportunity for bacteria to adapt and develop resistance. If that happens, the antibiotic may become less effective or stop working altogether, making infections harder to treat.
Antibiotic resistance is one part of the wider problem of antimicrobial resistance , or AMR. Other microbes, such as viruses, fungi and parasites, can also become resistant to the medicines used to treat them.
As healthcare professionals, we have a responsibility to make sure medicines such as antibiotics are prescribed appropriately. But everyone can play a part in helping to keep them working for the future.
This does not mean avoiding antibiotics when they are needed. It means using the right antibiotic, for the right patient, at the right time, and only for as long as needed. The UK Health Security Agency’s Andi Biotic , mascot of the Keep Antibiotics Working campaign, is one way this message is being shared.
Antibiotics and children
Many common childhood illnesses are caused by viruses and will get better without antibiotics. Antibiotics do not work against viral infections such as most coughs, colds and flu.
In Essex, 36.6% of children aged 0 to 9 received at least one antibiotic prescription from primary care in the past 12 months. The NHS England ambition is 25% or fewer by March 2027.
This is not about withholding antibiotics from children who need them. When antibiotics are needed to treat a bacterial infection, they can be essential. It is about avoiding antibiotics when they will not help, while making sure parents and carers know how to manage symptoms and when to seek further help. Your doctor, nurse or pharmacist can advise about the best treatment and what signs to look out for.
Everyone’s responsibility
Small actions today can help keep antibiotics working for our families and future generations.
We can all play our part by:
Using antibiotics wisely. Only take antibiotics when they have been prescribed for you, take them as directed and never save them for another time or share them with someone else. Pharmacists can also help with symptoms of coughs, colds and other minor illnesses.
Preventing infections spreading. Simple measures such as good hand hygiene and staying at home when you are unwell can help reduce the spread of infections.
Keeping vaccinations up to date. Getting the flu, RSV, COVID and other vaccinations you are eligible for helps protect you from serious illness and can reduce the chance of infections leading to hospital treatment.
Healthcare has responsibilities too. We need to continue improving prescribing, reviewing whether antibiotics are genuinely needed and learning from variation in prescribing between services and different parts of the country.

Od4eec.text:
Dagenham & Redbridge Football Club is saddened to hear of the passing of Patricia Mary Shaw.
Patricia dedicated over 30 years of her life to the club, both working and volunteering, and became a much-loved and familiar face to so many.
Whether behind the bar, preparing meals and looking after the players, or taking care of the boardroom, Patricia gave her time, care and dedication to the club throughout the years.
She was much more than a member of staff; she was part of the Dagenham & Redbridge family. Her commitment, kindness and contribution will always be remembered by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing her.
Our heartfelt condolences go to Patricia’s family and friends at this very sad time.
Rest in peace, Patricia. Thank you for everything. You will never be forgotten.

O897b1.title: Report: Southend 2-3 Boreham Wood
O897b1.text:
Fixtures
Southend United Vs. Boreham Wood - Fri, Nov 20th 2026, 19:45
Despite an improved second-half performance, three first-half goals from Boreham Wood proved the difference at Roots Hall, with Southend United losing 3-2 to the league leaders.
The visitors raced into a 3-0 lead by half-time thanks to a flurry of goals in the space of 14 minutes.
Oliver Bainbridge opened the scoring, drilling past Joe Duncan at his near post after being threaded through by Regan Booty.
The midfielder then set up Boreham Wood’s second as well, floating in a cross to the far post where Ben Whitfield slid in.
Former Shrimper, Zak Brunt added a third just past the half-hour mark from close range after being picked out by Whitfield.
Kieron Dyer’s substitutes made a difference in the second half, and two of them linked up to bring Blues back into the game, with Tyreece Simpson heading in Maxwell McKnight’s cross.
Instantly afterwards, the Shrimpers scored another with debutant Rico Richards’ drilled effort going in off the foot of the post.
Kick-Off
The away side had the first attempt of the game after just three minutes when Tylor Golden picked Kyle McAdam’s pocket and found Whitfield, whose shot from 20 yards went wide.
Just before the quarter of an hour mark, the Wood again threatened, and this time Joe Duncan had to make an excellent save to keep the game goalless.
Regan Booty’s free kick from 25 yards was whipped over the wall and forced a fine diving save from Duncan to push away. The danger wasn't yet clear though, with a backheel from Golden having to be headed off the line by McAdam.
The corner that then followed led to another scare with Charlie O’Connell getting free at the back post, but Wales international Duncan was again on hand to make a save.
After 19 minutes, Blues were finally breached with Bainbridge scoring his first goal of the campaign.
Booty threaded a clever pass into the left back, who had ghosted in behind the Shrimpers defence, and he cut inside onto his right foot and drilled a low effort past Duncan and into the bottom near corner.
Ten minutes later, Duncan again had to make another impressive stop, scrambling across his goal line to deny Matt Rush from close range after Tarryn Allarakhia had played a low ball across the six-yard box.
However, the danger hadn’t passed, with the visitors keeping possession and recycling play to double their lead.
Booty got his second assist of the evening as he floated a cross towards the far post where Whitfield was on hand to slide in and make it 2-0.
Four minutes later, the Wood’s lead was extended to three with former Shrimper Brunt returning to Roots Hall with a goal.
He initially played a ball over the top that released Whitfield in behind; the Barrow loanee was forced wide by Duncan, but he spotted the run of Brunt into the box and teed up his fellow midfielder, who slotted in a simple finish from six yards out.
Half-Time: Southend United 0-3 Boreham Wood
The Shrimpers made a triple substitution at half-time and, after 65 minutes, two of those who were introduced linked up to pull one back for Blues.
McKnight was found by Omochere, and he delivered a first-time cross which picked out Simpson whose downward header snuck under Ted Curd and in.
A second assist in Southend colours for McKnight and a third goal for Simpson, who both got goal contributions against Aldershot Town on Saturday.
This sparked some belief in the Shrimpers, and two minutes later another substitute got his name on the scoresheet – Richards on his debut.
Omochere was again involved; after receiving the ball from Dan Cox, the Bristol Rovers loanee played a pass on the turn to Richards, who let it run across his body before drilling a shot back across goal that went in off the foot of the post.
However, despite this, the Shrimpers were unable to score an equaliser and fell to a fourth defeat of the season.
Full-Time: Southend United 2-3 Boreham Wood

Oc85ca.title: These questions were at the heart of our 2026 symposium – Civil Society in a Changing Landscape
Oc85ca.text:
How can civil society respond to a changing landscape, and what will it take to build stronger communities across Greater Essex?
These questions were at the heart of our 2026 symposium, Civil Society in a Changing Landscape , held at Hatfield Place on 19 November. The event brought together members of the voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) sector, public sector leaders, health partners, funders and community representatives from across Greater Essex to explore the changes shaping civil society and consider how we can strengthen communities and shape what comes next.
Our Director of Programmes and Partnerships, Gavin Benn, opened the symposium, with Trustee Gail Cunningham hosting the day. In her opening address, A Changing Landscape , Gail reflected on A Joint Vision for Civil Society in Greater Essex and the partnerships it has helped build between ECF, local organisations and public sector partners. She highlighted the importance of better understanding the sector’s experiences and needs, which led to the commissioning of our Community Listening Project: VCSE Sector Audit 2026 .
Professor Tony Chapman of Durham University’s St Chad’s College presented the VCSE Sector Audit findings in Understanding Civil Society in Greater Essex . He explored the scale of the sector, its contribution to local communities and the pressures organisations face, including financial uncertainty, rising demand and difficulties recruiting and retaining people.
Despite these challenges, Tony was struck by the ambition and optimism of organisations across the sector. Reflecting on ECF’s ambitions, he remarked: “Your ambition is totally out of control!”
Emma de Closset, Chief Executive of UK Community Foundations, joined Gail for Greater Essex in National Context , discussing national pressures on civil society and opportunities for local collaboration. She praised the Joint Statement for Civil Society in Greater Essex as “such a wonderful innovation”, highlighting how bringing organisations together around shared goals could offer a model for other areas. She also described Greater Essex as “a real inspiration for place-based working and local convening”.
Dr Sebastien Chapleau, Community Organiser at Citizens UK, then led From Insight to Collective Action . Drawing on Citizens UK’s experience, he explored how building relationships around shared concerns can help communities strengthen their voice and influence change.
Click the photo below to see a full gallery of images from the day on Flickr.
Essex Community Foundation
Hatfield Place
After lunch, we gave attendees a first look at our #MyEssex campaign, ahead of its public launch.
The afternoon began with Resilience Through Change , as Gina Gardiner of Fatima’s UK Campaign reflected on how individuals, organisations and communities can navigate uncertainty and recognise their strengths. Maria Wilby from Refugee, Asylum and Migrant Action (RAMA) followed with Navigating Change: A Local Perspective , sharing insights into the opportunities and challenges facing organisations working directly with communities.
To close the day, ECF Trustee Maggie Desmond led Shaping What Comes Next . Drawing on the VCSE Sector Audit and the day’s discussions, she encouraged attendees to put the findings to use in their own work, involve local organisations earlier in decision-making and identify practical opportunities to work differently with others.
Thank you to everyone who joined us and contributed to the day’s discussions!

Behind Essex’s 5,200 voluntary, community and social enterprise organisations is a sector making a huge difference to local communities. But what does the evidence tell us about the challenges and opportunities shaping its future?
We’re excited to share that our Community Listening Project: VCSE Sector Audit 2026 is now available to read on our website.
Across Essex, these organisations contribute an estimated £4.6 billion in economic and social value, playing a significant role in supporting communities.
Bringing together quantitative research led by Professor Tony Chapman of Durham University and qualitative research by Hannah Fletcher, the VCSE Sector Audit draws on the experiences of organisations and public sector partners. It explores the sector’s contribution, how organisations operate across Essex, funding and financial resilience, the pressures facing staff and volunteers, and relationships with health services, public bodies and infrastructure support.

O7189a.title: Retail sales rise, but uneven recovery continues to challenge high street businesses
O7189a.text:
“One strong month isn’t a recovery”: the leading accountancy firm Price Bailey urges retailers to look beyond turnover ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.
The latest retail sales figures, released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) today, offer some encouragement for the retail sector, with total sales volumes increasing by 0.7% in October, outperforming economists’ expectations. Sales volumes also rose by 2.3% compared with October of last year.
However, accountancy firm Price Bailey says the headline figures mask a more uneven picture across the sector, with some retailers continuing to face challenging trading conditions despite the overall improvement.
Some of October’s growth appears to have been driven by increased supermarket purchases of long-life goods, including tinned food and UHT milk, following the Government’s Be Ready campaign. Food store sales volumes increased by 0.8% over the month.
Meanwhile, performance across non-food retail remains mixed. Although other non-food retailers recorded a 3.1% increase in sales volumes, department stores saw a 1.2% decline and household goods retailers experienced a 1% fall.
The figures also highlight the continued importance of online retail, with online sales values increasing by 9.7% year-on-year in October. Online spending now accounts for 29.2% of total retail sales, reinforcing the importance of digital channels as consumer shopping habits continue to evolve.
Stella Athanasiadou , Audit Partner and Retail sector specialist at Price Bailey, comments: “While the increase in retail sales is encouraging, it’s important not to mistake one month’s growth for a sustained recovery. The figures demonstrate just how varied trading conditions remain across the sector, with some retailers performing well while others continue to face considerable pressure.
“Online retail continues to grow, presenting both opportunities and challenges for traditional high street businesses. Retailers are having to think carefully about how they balance the costs of physical premises with the investment required to compete online, while ensuring that growth across different channels is translating into sustainable profits.
“As we approach the Christmas trading period, retailers should be looking beyond turnover and paying close attention to their cash flow, stock levels and profit margins. Understanding which products and sales channels are delivering the strongest returns, managing overheads and planning for different trading scenarios can all help businesses navigate uncertainty.
“Ultimately, those retailers that maintain strong financial discipline and understand their numbers will be better placed to withstand challenging conditions and take advantage of opportunities as they arise.”

Od8ab9.title: Essex mum avoids A&E visit thanks to local NHS eye care service
Od8ab9.text:
An Essex woman avoided a trip to A&E after getting help from a free NHS service for new eye problems.
The Minor Eye Conditions Service (MECS) helps people with eye problems that have started recently. It is available at participating opticians across Essex, without needing to see a GP first.
Jayne Mason, from Thurrock, discovered the service when her mum developed a red, painful eye.
Her mum was considering going to A&E, but Jayne first contacted her usual optician. When they could not offer an appointment, Jayne searched online and found another practice offering MECS in Pitsea.
After a short telephone assessment, her mum was offered an appointment within 30 minutes.
An optometrist, a healthcare professional who examines eyes, checked her symptoms and reassured her that there was no serious problem requiring further treatment.
“When I visited Mum, she had developed a red, painful eye and was considering going to A&E. Her usual optician couldn’t offer an appointment, so I searched online and found another local practice offering MECS.
“After a quick telephone assessment, Mum was offered an appointment, had a thorough examination and, most importantly, we were reassured that there was nothing seriously wrong.
“The whole experience was excellent. Mum got expert advice quickly and conveniently, and it meant we avoided an unnecessary trip to A&E. It’s a useful service for people to know about.”
Jayne said
How the NHS eye care service can help
The Minor Eye Conditions Service can assess and treat a range of new eye problems, including:
Red or sore eyes
Dry, gritty or uncomfortable eyes
Eye irritation or swelling
Watery eyes
New flashes or floaters in your vision
Eye pain
Ingrowing eyelashes
Small objects in the eye, such as grit
You do not need a referral from your GP.
The service is free for eligible patients and is available through participating optical practices across Essex.
“Jayne’s experience shows how the Minor Eye Conditions Service can help people get the right eye care quickly and closer to home.
“If you develop a new or recent problem with your eyes, such as redness, soreness, irritation or new flashes and floaters, you may be able to get help from a participating local optical practice without seeing your GP first.
“The optometrist will assess your symptoms and can provide treatment where appropriate. If you need care from another NHS service, they can advise you about what to do next.
“We want more people in Essex to know that this service is available and to consider it when they develop a new eye problem.”
Dr Boye Tayo, Clinical Lead for Eye Care at NHS Essex, said:
How to get an appointment
If you have a new eye problem, you can contact a participating optical practice directly.
Find a local practice offering the Minor Eye Conditions Service.
Call the practice and ask for a MECS appointment.
Answer some questions about your symptoms.
The practice will advise you about an appointment or what to do next.
Depending on your symptoms, you may be offered an appointment within 24 hours or within a few working days.
Call before visiting. Do not turn up without an appointment.
Find out more about the Minor Eye Conditions Service and how to get an appointment.
What patients say about the service
In a survey of 641 patients who used the service in mid and south Essex between April and June 2026:
96% said they would recommend it to family and friends.
35% said they would have gone to their GP without the service.
20% said they would have gone to A&E.
The results show how the service can help people find an alternative to visiting their GP or A&E for some eye problems.
When to get emergency help
ome eye problems need emergency medical attention.
Go to A&E or call 999 if:
You suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes.
You have severe eye pain.
You have a serious eye injury.
A sharp object has pierced your eye.
A strong chemical has gone into your eye.
If a strong chemical gets into your eye, keep rinsing it with water while wait

O4aa2f.title: Pre-Match Guide: Boreham Wood (H)
O4aa2f.text:
We’re looking forward to welcoming more than 9,700 supporters to Roots Hall for our top-of-the-table clash with league leaders Boreham Wood.
Only a handful of tickets remain in the home sections, with best availability in the wefinanceanycar.com South Stand Lower.
If you’re attending tonight’s match, please take a moment to read this guide to the game.
Parking & Access
There is no parking on-site at Roots Hall, and with a capacity crowd expected we expect heavy traffic around the surrounding roads, so we strongly advise supporters to arrive via public transport.
The easiest route to Southend is via c2c’s Shoeburyness – Fenchurch Street service, which stops at Southend Central; just a 20-minute walk from the stadium.
As a reminder, we have secured the land behind Roots Hall Avenue, so the only pedestrian access to the Main Car Park is through the Victoria Avenue entrance.
Away Tickets
Visiting supporters will only be able to purchase tickets in-person at the BTMK Box Office, and will need to provide evidence of one of the following:
ID showing a Hertfordshire postcode
Boreham Wood season ticket
At least two match tickets for a Boreham Wood fixture not involving Southend United
We expect the BTMK Box Office to be busy, so we advise visiting supporters wishing to purchase a ticket to arrive at least 90 minutes before kick-off.
Food & Drink
Pre-match food is available from Community Corner courtesy of Eat Street and Flour Power.
The Shrimpers Bar opens from 5:15pm, while the Far Post Bar and Groundsman’s Bar open with the rest of the stadium’s bars and kiosks at 6:15pm.
Our real ale offering is provided by Brentwood Brewery Company, available from the Shrimpers Bar, Far Post Bar, Groundsman’s Bar, and West Main Bar.
Weather permitting, our self-service bar in the external concourse of the Gilbert & Rose Stand will be open as well.
The Blue Eagle is open all afternoon and evening, with karaoke taking place from 6:30pm until 10:30pm.
Match Programmes
This week’s edition of The Shrimper stars Tyreece Simpson as he reflects on his days as a rugby prodigy, breakthrough into professional football, and the freedom he feels playing for Southend United under Kieron Dyer.
There are also features on tonight’s visitors, our popular 1998/99 home kit, and Southend United Ladies forward Zoe Tryfonos.
Programmes are available to purchase by card from the Club Shop, The Blue Eagle, and all food and drink kiosks and bars around the stadium, and by cash from our dedicated team of programme sellers.
Following the high demand for Aldershot Town’s edition, there are also a limited number of programmes from last Saturday’s fixture available from the Club Shop and programme sellers outside the Climatec Group East Stand.

O6e278.title: London Stansted to conduct major emergency training exercise
O6e278.text:
An emergency training exercise designed to test London Stansted’s response to a major aircraft accident will take place next week as part of the airport's regular preparedness programme.
The exercise will be held on Tuesday 24 November and forms part of the airport's four-year regulatory testing programme. The exercise is required under Civil Aviation Authority regulations, which require UK certificated aerodromes to undertake a full-scale aircraft accident exercise at least once every four years.
Local residents and passengers are being advised in advance of the exercise, so they are not alarmed on the day by the high number of emergency service vehicles in the area.
The scenario will simulate an aircraft accident requiring a complex, prolonged, multi-agency response and is designed to test life-saving procedures, command and control arrangements, communications, and support processes for passengers, families and stakeholders.
The exercise will take place at the airport's Compass Base facility, a remote aircraft parking stand, using a decommissioned aircraft and has been carefully planned to ensure there is no impact on flight operations or passengers using the airport. A number of emergency service vehicles and personnel will be visible in the area during the exercise.
Around 400 participants will take part, including teams from across London Stansted, alongside colleagues from Essex Police, Essex County Fire & Rescue Service, East of England Ambulance Service and Essex & Herts Air Ambulance.
Also supporting the exercise will be the British Red Cross, Uttlesford District Council, Essex County Council, the Rapid Relief Team, the Air Accident Investigation Branch, the Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government, Ryanair, Border Force and National Express.
Nick Millar, Operations Director at London Stansted Airport, said:
"The safety and security of our passengers, colleagues and airport community is always our highest priority.
"Although an aircraft accident is an extremely unlikely event, it remains the most significant emergency scenario we could face, which is why it is vital that we regularly test our plans, procedures and response capabilities.
"The exercise will bring together airport teams, emergency services and partner organisations from across the region, giving us the opportunity to rehearse how we would work together in a highly challenging situation and identify any opportunities to strengthen our response arrangements.
"We want to reassure passengers, local residents and businesses that this is only a training exercise and there will be no impact on the airport's day-to-day operations. However, people in the area may notice increased activity from emergency service vehicles and personnel on the day."
Essex Police Chief Inspector Julia Finch, Stansted Airport Commander , said:
"We regularly test our plans and capabilities, and this is no exception.
"Taking part in these exercises are really important to ensure we are ready for any eventuality, no matter how unlikely the scenario.
"We have a really positive working relationship with Stansted Airport and we’re grateful for this opportunity."
The exercise is designed to provide assurance that emergency plans, facilities, people and partner organisations can work effectively together under realistic conditions and operational pressures, in addition to fulfilling the airport's regulatory requirements.

O674a2.title: Get your flu vaccine now to help protect yourself and your loved ones this Christmas
O674a2.source: NHS England East of England news
O674a2.text:
NHS organisations across the East of England are jointly urging anyone eligible for a free flu vaccination to get it now if they have not yet had it this winter. The call comes ahead of spending time with family and friends this Christmas.
The flu vaccine can take up to two weeks to build protection. NHS Essex, NHS Central East and NHS Norfolk and Suffolk are encouraging residents to get vaccinated by Friday 11 December to give the vaccine time to work before Christmas Day.
Christmas is a time when families and friends come together, and flu can spread easily through close contact. Getting vaccinated helps reduce your risk of serious illness. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to family members, including those at greater risk of becoming seriously unwell.
Older people, pregnant women and people with certain long-term health conditions are particularly at risk of serious illness from flu. Getting vaccinated helps reduce that risk.
Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex, said:  “As you make your Christmas plans, please make time for your flu vaccination too. Flu can make anyone unwell, but for some people it can lead to serious complications, a hospital stay and, in some cases, death. If you’re eligible for a free vaccine and haven’t had it yet, book an appointment now rather than leaving it until the festive rush.
“If you’re a parent or carer, please also check whether your eligible child has had their flu vaccine. If they’ve missed it, make arranging their vaccination part of your Christmas preparations.
“If you can only get an appointment after 11 December, please still take it. Flu can circulate well beyond Christmas, and vaccination can help protect you through the rest of winter.”
Dr Katherine Rowe, Deputy Clinical Director at NHS Central East, said: “Christmas brings different generations together, including older people, pregnant women and those with certain long-term health conditions, for whom flu can be particularly serious.
If you’re eligible, taking up your free flu vaccine is an important step in reducing your risk of serious illness. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to family members. Please make vaccination part of looking after yourself and your loved ones this Christmas.”
Lisa Nobes, Executive Director of Nursing, NHS Norfolk and Suffolk ICB, said: “If you’re eligible for a free NHS flu vaccination, a participating pharmacy can help you get protected ahead of Christmas. Some pharmacies offer walk-in vaccinations, so you may not need to book an appointment.
“Please check with your local pharmacy about availability before travelling. The chances are, there’s one near you offering the vaccination.
“It’s a busy time of year for most of us, but our health and wellbeing is worth making a bit of time for, alongside all our Christmas preparations. I want people to be able to enjoy the festive season and not be in bed, or in hospital, with flu.”
Dr Eleanor Powers, Head of Public Health Commissioning (immunisation) for NHS England – East of England, said: “Last year, around 104,000 hospitalisations were avoided through people getting their jabs and protecting themselves, their loved ones, our communities and helping the NHS prepare for winter.
“So far this season, over 2 million people in the East of England have already had their flu jab, which is great news, but there are plenty more appointments available.
“The flu jab really is your best defence against winter illness. It takes just a few minutes, but it can protect you for months, helping to prevent serious illness, avoid hospital admissions and keeping the most vulnerable people safe.
“Now is also a great time to get your 2- and 3-year-olds vaccinated; little ones can get really unwell with flu. Ob7515.title: Crews extinguish fire at scrapyard
Ob7515.text:
Crews extinguish fire at scrapyard
Dom Bowers
7:21am 20 Nov 2026
Date
6.08pm - 20 November 2026
Crews extinguish fire at scrapyard
Crews extinguished a fire at a scrapyard in Little Thurrock.
We were called to Rectory Road yesterday (Thursday 19 November) at 6.08pm and found about 80 tonnes of scrap metal alight.
About 20 firefighters tackled the fire. They extinguished it by 8.50pm and worked with site staff to break up the material and check for hotspots.
Crews left the scene at 9.30pm.
It is believed the fire was caused by a discarded battery.
Station Manager Rick Williams said: "This incident highlights how important it is to dispose of batteries properly, not in a skip or with your general rubbish.
"Batteries can ignite if they are damaged or crushed, so please take used batteries to a recycling centre or collection point."
Visit loveessex.org to find your nearest recycling facility.

Oe52a4.title: How to return crutches, frames and other mobility equipment to ESNEFT
Oe52a4.source: East Suffolk & North Essex NHS (Colchester Hospital)
Oe52a4.text:
Returning mobility equipment
Patients who have been given mobility equipment to use are being asked to return it when no longer needed.
Crutches, metal walking sticks and walking frames are among some of the items patients can return if they’ve borrowed the equipment or been issued the equipment from Ipswich or Colchester hospitals.
Each item of equipment is deep cleaned, checked and maintained or repaired before being issued to another patient.
Items that can be returned include:
Crutches
metal walking sticks
walking frames
perching stools
commodes
shower chairs
toilet frames
How you return equipment is different depending on the area.
Returning equipment in east Suffolk/Ipswich:
Drop it into the large blue recycling container outside Entrance 6 or the Garrett Anderson building at Ipswich Hospital (you can park for free in the drop off bay if quickly returning equipment in the container)
Contact Suffolk Medequip for a free collection. Arrange a collection by phone on 01473 351 805 or email Suffolk Medequip.
Take it to Medequip’s depot at Unit 31, Bluestem Road, Ransomes Europark, Ipswich, IP3 9RR
Return it to the Live Well Hub in Leiston at Waterloo Centre, Waterloo Avenue, Leiston, IP16 4HF
Return it to The Dales in Ipswich at 216 Dales Road, Ipswich, IP1 4JY.
Returning equipment in north Essex/Colchester:
Return crutches, walking frames and metal walking sticks to the large blue recycling container outside the front entrance of Colchester Hospital or to the large blue recycling containers outside the side entrance doors to the ESEOC Dame Clare Marx Building at Colchester Hospital.
Any medical equipment that was delivered directly to your house should have a Medequip or ECL sticker on it. If so, you can contact Medequip for a free collection. Their details are listed below.
Phone 0333 034 2048, or  email Essex Medequip via email.
This includes:
hospital beds
toilet frames
perching stools
commodes
hoists
slings
slide sheets
wendylet (special bed sheet) etc.
You can also return equipment with an ECL or Medequip sticker direct to the depot at Unit 2, Horizon 120 Business Park, Horizon Boulevard, Braintree, Essex, CM77 7AY.
If you’ve left Colchester Hospital with a piece of medical equipment that isn’t a walking aid and doesn’t have a Medequip or ECL sticker on it, please do not return it to Medequip but contact the team at the hospital who supplied it.
Material moon boots or arm supports cannot be returned as they cannot be cleaned for future patients.
Please don’t return equipment to our community hospitals or to our community teams – they aren’t able to take back equipment there.

O2c41b.title: Get your flu vaccine before Christmas
O2c41b.text:
If you are eligible for a free NHS flu vaccine and have not had it yet, book your appointment now.
The vaccine can take up to two weeks to build protection. Getting vaccinated by Friday 11 December will give it time to work before Christmas Day.
If you cannot get an appointment by then, you should still have the vaccine. Flu can spread throughout winter.
Why the flu vaccine matters
Christmas is a time when families and friends come together. This can make it easier for flu to spread.
Flu can make anyone unwell. For some people, it can cause serious illness and lead to a stay in hospital.
People at greater risk include older people, pregnant women and people with certain long-term health conditions. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to other family members.
As you make your Christmas plans, please make time for your flu vaccination too. Flu can make anyone unwell, but for some people it can lead to serious complications, a hospital stay and, in some cases, death. If you’re eligible for a free vaccine and haven’t had it yet, book an appointment now rather than leaving it until the festive rush.
If you’re a parent or carer, please also check whether your eligible child has had their flu vaccine. If they’ve missed it, make arranging their vaccination part of your Christmas preparations.
If you can only get an appointment after 11 December, please still take it. Flu can circulate well beyond Christmas, and vaccination can help protect you through the rest of winter.
Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex
How to get your flu vaccine
Eligible adults can:
book through the NHS website or NHS App
call 119 free of charge if they cannot book online
ask their GP practice about appointments
ask a participating pharmacy about appointments.
Some pharmacies offer walk-in vaccinations. Check with the pharmacy before travelling.
If you are pregnant, you can also ask your midwife about getting vaccinated.
Flu vaccines for children
Children who were aged two or three on 31 August 2026 can get their free flu vaccine at their GP practice or a participating pharmacy.
From 1 December 2026 , children from Reception to Year 11 who missed their flu vaccination at school can also get vaccinated at a participating pharmacy.
Parents and carers can ask the pharmacy about appointments or contact their school vaccination team about a catch-up appointment.
Last year, around 104,000 hospitalisations were avoided through people getting their jabs and protecting themselves, their loved ones, our communities and helping the NHS prepare for winter.
So far this season, over 2 million people in the East of England have already had their flu jab, which is great news, but there are plenty more appointments available.
The flu jab really is your best defence against winter illness. It takes just a few minutes, but it can protect you for months, helping to prevent serious illness, avoid hospital admissions and keeping the most vulnerable people safe.
Now is also a great time to get your 2- and 3-year-olds vaccinated; little ones can get really unwell with flu. Many people don’t know that whilst school age children get their offer in their schools, younger children age 2 and 3 are also entitled to a nasal spray vaccine and they can get it at their GP or at a participating local pharmacy.
Now it is easier than ever to book – there are plenty of appointments available at the time and place most convenient to you giving you and your family the best possible protection over Christmas and through the winter months.”
Dr Eleanor Powers, Head of Public Health Commissioning (immunisation) for NHS England – East of England

O3e543.title: Preview: Boreham Wood (H)
O3e543.text:
Friday night football returns to Roots Hall as Southend United face their toughest test of the season so far as the unbeaten league leaders Boreham Wood travel to South Essex.
The Shrimpers returned to winning ways last weekend with a 2-1 comeback against Aldershot Town and will be looking to record back-to-back home wins for the first time since September.
THE VISITORS
The Enterprise National League leaders, Boreham Wood, have bounced back superbly from last season’s promotion final defeat to enjoy a faultless start to this campaign.
Most of last season’s squad has stuck around, which, along with a few new faces, has set the groundwork for another strong campaign.
They did, however, lose exciting playmaker Abdul Abdulmalik to Swedish first division side Djurgårdens for a National League record sale of £1.5 million.
Despite the departure of the 18-goal midfielder in August, the Wood are on course to enjoy an even better season this time around.
They are still unbeaten this term, with their last league defeat in the regular season coming in a 4-1 drubbing at Solihull Moors on Easter Monday.
This season got off to a slightly frustrating start, conceding in the 12 th minute of stoppage time to draw 3-3 at home to Tamworth.
This was then followed by a five-game winning run before being held to a draw by Eastleigh in mid-September.
After losing 3-0 to Wigan Athletic in the Emirates FA Cup a fortnight ago, the Wood almost lost their unbeaten league record last weekend, but Lewis Richardson rescued a point against Yeovil Town with ten minutes to play; they were also aided by a late Yeovil penalty miss in the 84 th minute.
WHEN WE’VE MET BEFORE
The Shrimpers have only won one of our last five contests with Boreham Wood – a 4-2 victory at Roots Hall on Easter Monday 2024 which pushed the Wood closer to relegation to the sixth tier.
Last season, Josh Walker came off the bench to score his first goal since the opening day to rescue a point at Meadow Park, whilst at Roots Hall, former Shrimper Matt Rush was on target in a 2-0 defeat.
In total, Blues have won four of the six meetings the two sides have had at Roots Hall, with the first coming in the FA Cup in 1973/74.
PLAYED FOR BOTH
Three former Shrimpers now ply their trade with the Wood.
Matt Rush and Zak Brunt, who have the most goals and assists in the division respectively, and defender Ollie Kensdale.
In the Southend ranks, Ben Goodliffe previously represented Boreham Wood.

The gaffer is urging for a fast start from his side and for the 9,400 plus Shrimpers to get behind the team under the lights.
"We've got to be full of intensity and purpose and if we do that, with our crowd, it can make Boreham Wood very uncomfortable."

O1ccdc.title: Local Swimmers Cross the English Channel and Raise Over £9,000 for Havens Hospices
O1ccdc.text:
A group of five friends from Burnham-on-Crouch challenged themselves by embarking on an open water relay swim across the English Channel in aid of a local hospice charity.
James Cliff, Andrew Bell, Madeline Raymond, Clare Boston and Stuart Sargeant, also known as the Burnham Gang, finished their relay in 10 hours and 50 minutes whilst fundraising for Havens Hospices. So far, they have raised over £9,000 to support the charity in providing expert, compassionate care to local children and adults of all ages living with incurable conditions.
The route is around 21 miles long across one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, with powerful tidal movements, strong currents and cold water at temperatures of around 18°C.
The group made the decision to take on this challenge after visiting Fair Havens and Little Havens, the charity’s hospices for adults and children, and learning about the care they provide to families within the local community.
James, who also fundraised for the charity in 2023 by swimming across the English Channel solo, said, “We are keen open water swimmers and after seeing the incredible work of hospices firsthand by visiting Havens Hospices, we decided to fundraise by setting a hard challenge that would also stay with us as an amazing group memory.
“Standout memories were certainly made. Seasickness, jellyfish stings, swimming in the dark and narrowly avoiding big tankers! We swam on the night of the Harvest Moon and as we got to Cap Gris-Nez, it shone out at us just by the famous lighthouse.
“We’re all so pleased to have completed this challenge and knowing it was making a real difference to families helped get us through the tough moments.
“To all first-time fundraisers, it’s never too early to start fundraising ahead of your challenge. Don’t be afraid to keep asking and be inventive.”
Lucy Lock, Community Engagement Manager at Havens Hospices, said, “We want to say a huge thank you to the Burnham Gang. Swimming the English Channel through the night, with jellyfish, seasickness and tankers to contend with, is an incredible achievement, and we’re so grateful they chose to do it in aid of Havens Hospices.
“All of our care and support is provided absolutely free of charge, and we rely on the generosity of our community to make that possible. The money the Burnham Gang have raised goes towards expert, compassionate care for local families, whether that’s in our hospices, in the comfort of their own homes or out in the community, making every day count for the people who need us.”
The Burnham Gang are now calling on the local community to support them in their quest to continue raising vital funds for Havens Hospices by making a donation to their JustGiving page. The charity must raise more than £225,000 a week to be there for everyone who needs them, so every donation, no matter how small, will make a difference in supporting the hospice charity.
You can support the Burnham Gang’s fundraising efforts by donating to their JustGiving page: https://www.justgiving.com/page/burnhamrelay

Ofd816.title: Provide Community invited to help pilot the UK’s first nursing and midwifery public health framework
Ofd816.text:
We have been invited to help pilot the UK’s first Nursing and Midwifery Public Health Practice Framework. The framework recognises how nurses, midwives and nursing associates help people stay well, prevent illness and reduce health inequalities through the care they provide every day.
In community services, that might mean spotting early signs that someone’s health is getting worse, making health information easier to understand or working with local partners to help people get the support they need closer to home.
Professor Lucy Wightman, Chief Executive of Provide Health and Group Chief Nurse, said, “A routine appointment may be the first time someone tells us they are struggling to manage a condition at home or explains what’s making it difficult to get help.
“Listening and acting on what they tell us can help prevent problems from getting worse. The framework recognises the skill involved in that everyday work and gives teams a way to share what works.”
Published on Monday 16 November 2026, the framework was developed with contributions from all four UK nations and endorsed by their Chief Nursing Officers. It gives nurses and midwives across the UK, and nursing associates in England, a shared approach to five areas of practice: promoting wellbeing, protecting people from harm, preventing ill health, working in partnership to reduce inequalities and supporting environmentally sustainable care.
Mark Heasman, Group Chief Executive of Provide Community, added, “Our teams see first-hand what helps people get the care they need and where they still face barriers. Taking part in the pilot would give us a chance to share that experience, learn from other organisations and use what we learn to make our own services easier to access.”
We are due to meet with the Florence Nightingale Foundation, which supports the pilot programme, to discuss how the pilot could work. Activity could begin in January 2027, subject to those discussions.

O3f52e.title: Disabled Children: Access to Therapy - [Emma Lewell in the Chair] | Backbench Business | Westminster Hall debates
O3f52e.text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Ms Lewell. I start by thanking my hon. Friend the Member for Bexleyheath and Crayford (Daniel Francis) for securing this incredibly passionate and well-informed debate. I know this issue is personal for him, and he talks about it with such passion both in Westminster Hall and in the main Chamber. I thank him for that, and for mentioning Harlow so many times in his speech. I also thank my two work experience students, Gaby and Tamsin, who are in the Public Gallery, for providing me with a very useful briefing. Members from across the House will agree that I am better briefed than I normally am—no comments.
I thank David from NAPA, who is also in the Gallery. I first came across NAPA when David kindly invited me to visit his clinic in Harlow. I was blown away and very emotional about the work done there, and I was incredibly keen to invite some of my parliamentary colleagues to visit NAPA. I am pleased that the Minister for Equalities and my hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) , who has a constituent who attends NAPA, had the opportunity to visit and see at first hand the work that David and his staff do.
What struck me more than the work I saw with the young people at the clinic was a graph—a very simple graph showing a bump and then a larger bump—of quality-adjusted life years for young people with cerebral palsy, and David explained how it was improving. We recognise that people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities will always have challenges in their lives, but NAPA is working to increase that quality of life. Ultimately, is that not what we want for everyone—to have the best possible quality of life?
I believe that the way we improve quality of life for young disabled people is through work on early intervention and specialist support. David’s colleagues use really innovative techniques to improve young people’s balance. Although I recognise the fantastic work that the Government have done to bring down waiting lists, as of September this year there are still 18,000 young people waiting for occupational therapy, 20,000 waiting for physiotherapy and 50,000 waiting for speech and language therapy. I welcome the work the Government have done so far, but there is clearly more to be done.
I want to talk briefly about some of the challenges and barriers. I again pay tribute to NAPA, which has worked with 344 children across the UK. I had the opportunity to speak to one family who came from Harrogate, and they talked about the significant logistical challenges. The parents have another son, so they had to take it in turns to travel from Harrogate to Harlow to visit NAPA. Obviously, during that time, they had to spend money to stay in a hotel, which is obviously an additional cost. My hon. Friend the Member for Bexleyheath and Crayford mentioned his 110-mile round trip, and that is the reality in terms of affordability, the postcode lottery and the geographical challenges. The barriers are clearly great.
David spoke to me about his son Angus, who was born in 2017. David saw at first hand how hard it was to get physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy for a disabled child, as we have mentioned. David was taught how to use a feeding tube, so that Angus could be fed at home through his nose. Between 2018 and 2023, he and his family had to travel to NAPA in Boston 15 times for therapy. Obviously, that comes at a huge cost. We thank David for bringing NAPA to the UK, and particularly for bringing it to Harlow.
There are challenges, but there is still plenty to be positive about in the Government’s approach. We know they have a 10-year health policy to shift care from hospitals into the community. We also know the work this Government are doing to reform SEND by investing over £40 million over three years to develop educational psychology and speech and language therapy, which is another development that we should welcome.

O4a016.title: Business National Emergency Briefing
O4a016.text:
Colchester Institute collaborated with Colchester-based PR and marketing consultancy Mosaic – The Conscience Marketing Agency to host a special screening of The People’s Emergency Briefing. The event brought local businesses together to learn more about climate change, share ideas and explore what they can do to make a difference.
Held on Wednesday 18th November, the event followed a debate in Westminster on Monday 16th November, where around 75 MPs came together to discuss calls for a government-led national emergency briefing on climate change and nature loss.
The debate received support from across political parties, with the Minister for Climate Transition, Katie White, agreeing to meet with the National Emergency Briefing organisers to discuss the next steps. However, the Government has not yet committed to delivering a national briefing.
Presented by wildlife presenter and environmentalist Chris Packham, The People’s Emergency Briefing looks at how climate change is affecting our everyday lives. From the impact on food supplies and public health to the risks to the economy and national security, the film highlights why acting now matters.
Following the screening, guests heard from a panel of local experts, chaired by Gemma Rawlinson, Managing Director at Mosaic. The panel included Becky Baines from Green Growth Ltd, Dr Jeremy Dagley from Essex Wildlife Trust and Marie-Ann Capps, Sustainability & Climate Change Officer at Colchester City Council.
The discussion focused on what the evidence means for Essex businesses and communities, and the practical steps organisations can take to reduce their environmental impact and become more resilient.
Gemma Rawlinson, Managing Director at Mosaic, said, “The debate in Westminster is encouraging, but businesses also need to think seriously about their own risks. If your business or a key supplier was affected by extreme weather, how would your organisation cope? We wanted to give people the opportunity to consider questions like this, share their experiences and learn from others who are already acting.”
The event also gave local businesses the opportunity to network and showcase their own sustainability efforts. Exhibition stands included Mosaic, Steven Eagell Toyota, Paddy & Scott’s, Fairfield’s Farm and Essex Wildlife Trust.
As North Essex’s largest vocational college, Colchester Institute plays an important role in the local community by building strong connections with businesses and providing students with the skills and knowledge they need for their future careers. Sustainability is an important part of this, with the College committed to reducing its environmental impact and helping to create a greener future.
The College is already making great progress. In the last academic year, Colchester Institute reduced its carbon emissions by an impressive 31%. This brings its total reductions to 55% since declaring a climate emergency and beginning to monitor emissions in 2020–21.
Gary Horne MBE, Deputy Chief Executive at Colchester Institute, said, “Climate change affects us all, but there are important questions that every business leader needs to be asking about how it could affect their organisation. Whether it’s extreme weather disrupting operations, rising costs or the impact on employees and customers, businesses need to understand the risks and think seriously about how they prepare.”
Further events are planned, including another in December.
More details on future events can be found at www.colchester.ac.uk/sustainability/ .

O6d48b.title: New way to complete waiting list questionnaires through My Alex Health
O6d48b.text:
We are changing the way we send digital questionnaires to adult patients who are waiting for treatment.
The questionnaires, previously sent through Healthcare Communications Envoy, will now be available through My Alex Health , our secure patient portal. This change will help make our communications more consistent, familiar and easier for patients to recognise.
What to expect
If you are an adult waiting for treatment and meet the relevant criteria, we will send you a questionnaire every 12 weeks. It lets you know that we are aware you are still waiting and gives you an opportunity to confirm whether you still need to be seen by the relevant specialty or whether you no longer require care from us.
The questionnaire takes around two minutes to complete. If you do not complete the questionnaire, your care will continue and you will remain on the waiting list.
How to access the questionnaire
You will receive a text message from ‘NHS PAHT’ asking you to complete the questionnaire in My Alex Health . If you are already registered, the message will explain how to access it. If you have not yet registered, you will receive a separate message with information to help you sign up. You can read more about the benefits here >
My Alex Health is our secure online patient portal, where patients can access information about their care with us and complete assessments and questionnaires from home.
If you do not feel confident completing the questionnaire online, you do not need to worry. Your care will continue and you will remain on the waiting list. You can ask a trusted family member, friend or carer to help you complete it if you wish.
Questionnaires for children and young people
For now, this questionnaire will only be sent to adult patients. We plan to develop a separate questionnaire for children and young people in the future.

Ob51b4.title: Employee owners help ten charities benefit from Provide Community grants
Ob51b4.text:
In October 2026, ten charities and community groups supporting people in areas served by Provide Community have received funding through its partnership with Ormiston Families , with employee owners helping decide where the money goes.
The initiative originally offered up to six grants of up to £5,000 to support charities and community groups. But after a closely contested members’ vote, Provide Community extended the funding so that all ten shortlisted organisations would benefit.
The five groups receiving the most votes have been awarded up to £5,000 each, with the remaining five receiving £2,000 each.
Applications were reviewed by Provide Community’s charity panel, made up of Member Representatives, a Non-Executive Director and our Company Secretary, which agreed a shortlist before inviting members to vote for the causes they wanted to support.
As an employee-owned community interest company, Provide Community gives colleagues a voice in the organisation and how it supports its communities. This initiative put that ownership into practice, enabling members to help direct funding towards causes that matter to them.
The following organisations have been awarded up to £5,000 each:
Brave Futures
Brighter Opportunities for Special People (BOSP)
Taking Baby Steps CIC
Sanctus
Assure (Lighthouse Family Trust)
A further £2,000 each has been awarded to:
Breast Friends CIC
Footsteps Walking With You
The Pear Tree Fund
Open Country
Hackney Foodbank
The close voting reflected the strong support for causes across the shortlist. Extending the funding means every shortlisted organisation will receive a contribution towards its work.
Mark Heasman, Group Chief Executive at Provide Community, said: “Being employee owned means our colleagues have a real say in how we support our communities. This vote gave our members the opportunity to champion causes that matter to them.
“With the votes so close, we wanted to recognise the support for all ten shortlisted organisations. We are delighted to extend the funding so that every one of them can benefit and we look forward to hearing about the difference these grants make.”
Delivered through the partnership with Ormiston Families, the grants form part of Provide Community’s wider commitment as a Community Interest Company, to reinvesting in the communities where it delivers services, extending its support beyond the care it provides.
Thank you to every organisation that applied, to the charity panel for reviewing the applications and to all members who took part in the vote. Together, they have helped turn employee ownership into practical support for ten community causes.

O4e005.title: Use antibiotics wisely and help keep them working
O4e005.text:
Antibiotics save lives, and we can all help keep them working. By choosing to use antibiotics wisely and only taking them when they are needed, people in Essex can help protect these important medicines for the future.
Antibiotic resistance is increasing. This happens when bacteria change and antibiotics no longer work as well against them. It can make infections much harder to treat.
In 2025, an average of 406 antibiotic-resistant bloodstream infections were reported each week in England. Some of these infections can be life-threatening.
When antibiotics can help
Antibiotics treat infections caused by bacteria. This includes some serious illnesses, such as pneumonia, meningitis and sepsis. They are also important for surgery and some cancer treatments.
Antibiotics do not work against viruses. This means they will not treat colds, flu or COVID-19.
Taking antibiotics when they are not needed can allow bacteria to become resistant. These bacteria can spread to other people and cause infections that are harder to treat.
What you can do
You can help keep antibiotics working:
Do not expect or demand antibiotics for common illnesses such as colds and flu.
Ask a pharmacist for advice about treating your symptoms.
Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed.
Never share antibiotics with another person.
Do not save antibiotics to use later.
Take leftover antibiotics to a pharmacy for safe disposal.
Have the vaccinations you are eligible for.
Wash your hands regularly.
Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue, then put it in a bin.
Stay at home when you are unwell, where possible.
These actions can reduce infections and unnecessary antibiotic use.
Protecting antibiotics for the future
We all have a role to play in halting the growth of antibiotic resistance. Please don’t go to your GP or other health professional expecting or demanding antibiotics. Instead, follow tried and tested advice for easing symptoms of common illnesses like colds and flu. You can visit the NHS website for further advice or can ask your pharmacist.
If you are prescribed antibiotics, please take them exactly as prescribed. Do not save them for later or share them with anyone else. If you do have any leftover antibiotics, take them to your pharmacist to dispose of them properly. And everyone who is eligible for vaccinations like flu, COVID-19 or RSV should make sure to arrange their vaccine.
If we all work towards protecting our antibiotics, we can make sure that we can continue to use them when they are needed.
Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex
You can also choose a personal pledge through the Antibiotic Guardian campaign. A pledge could be to use antibiotics only as advised or to return leftover antibiotics to a pharmacy.

O76c1c.title: Havens Hospices launches school Santa Run campaign
O76c1c.text:
Havens Hospices is calling on local schools to organise a Santa Run, encouraging pupils to don their best festive outfits and run, walk or skip to raise funds for its expert, compassionate care.
The Essex charity has launched its Santa Run campaign, asking schools to become festive fundraisers by picking a date in December, running a route of their choice and setting up a JustGiving page to raise sponsorship.
Participation is free, and each school will receive a downloadable fundraising pack when they sign up. Resources include a poster template, an assembly video explaining Havens Hospices’ care, a certificate for those taking part, and a letter to parents and carers explaining how schools’ support makes a difference.
The charity encourages pupils and teachers to get in the Christmas spirit by wearing Santa hats, Christmas jumpers, or festive fancy dress. To make the campaign sustainable and low-cost, Havens Hospices suggests using what pupils already have at home.
By taking part, schools can help Little Havens Hospice support more children like Teddy to make every day of their lives count.
Teddy was diagnosed with Dravet syndrome at four years old, and Little Havens has supported his family ever since.
Jasmine, Teddy’s mum, says, “Little Havens provides a safe space where all of Teddy’s needs are met. If we didn’t have Little Havens, our lives would be very difficult.”
Havens Hospices must raise more than £225,000 each week to support families like Teddy’s.
£31 could pay for an hour of expert care at Little Havens, providing care during a respite break, emergency stay or support at the end of a child’s/ or young person’s life.
£50 could provide a session of complementary therapy for someone we care for, helping them to relax, ease anxiety and even reduce pain caused by their condition.
£160 could provide a pool session at Little Havens with two of our Care Team, or a family swim session. Children can feel weightless and move more freely, while lights, floats, and bubbles offer rich sensory experiences, helping reduce stress and relax tense muscles.
Schools can find out more or sign up to the Santa Run campaign here: havenshospices.org.uk/christmas/santa-run

O4c735.title: Council shares suicide prevention work in Parliament
O4c735.text:
Epping Forest District Council (EFDC) was invited to Westminster to share its work on suicide prevention in the workplace at a parliamentary roundtable hosted by Liz Twist MP and the British Standards Institution (BSI).
Suicide and the Workplace standard
EFDC’s Public Health Apprentice and Service Director for Communities attended the event on 12 November at Portcullis House in the House of Commons, where they presented a case study on the council’s implementation of the BS 30480 Suicide and the Workplace.
The roundtable brought together more than 60 representatives from a wide range of sectors including the NHS, construction, higher education, aviation, banking, manufacturing, retail, the armed forces and suicide prevention charities to discuss how organisations can embed the standard to better support employees affected by suicide.
From left to right – Ezra Hewing Head of Centre for London for James’ Place Charity, Fabrizio Ferrari Service Director, Communities for Epping Forest District Council, Laura Cleverley Public Health Apprentice for Epping Forest District Council, Liz Twist MP for Blaydon and Consett,
Jane Packer Head of Standards at BSI
and Anne Hayes Director of Standards Development at BSI.
Suicide prevention and postvention measures
The discussion marked the first anniversary of the publication of the British Standard and explored both the opportunities and challenges organisations face when introducing suicide prevention and postvention measures in the workplace. EFDC representatives shared learning from the council’s journey so far, including the cultural changes being developed through its Suicide and the Workplace Working Group.
Compassionate and supportive workplace culture
The council’s work began following feedback gathered from suicide awareness sessions delivered earlier this year, which highlighted that many people felt workplaces were not sufficiently prepared to support staff affected by suicide. This insight led to the council adopting BS 30480 and establishing a dedicated working group to help embed its principles across the organisation.
The working group includes colleagues from Public Health, Human Resources, Community Resilience and specialist partner organisations, all working together to create a compassionate and supportive workplace culture.
Helping to start important conversations
During the roundtable, delegates highlighted the importance of taking a sensitive, authentic and people-led approach to implementing the standard, recognising that every organisation has its own culture and challenges. Participants also discussed how introducing even small elements of the standard can help start important conversations and improve support for employees.
Epping Forest District Council hopes its experience will encourage other organisations across the district and beyond to consider adopting elements of the standard and strengthening their own approach to suicide prevention, intervention and support for people affected by suicide.

Od35d1.title: East of England tops regional export growth rankings
Od35d1.text:
·       Six in ten exporters increased overseas sales in Q3 — the highest proportion among the four regions covered
·       42% entered a new overseas market, joint highest alongside London
·       US leads the region’s overseas growth markets, followed by France and Australia
The East of England recorded the highest proportion of firms growing overseas sales in the last quarter, according to the latest UK Trade Barometer.
Six in 10 exporters (60%) said they increased sales to existing overseas markets in Q3, ahead of London (59%), the Midlands (55%) and the North (53%), and above the UK-wide figure of 53%.
The region also shared the top spot for breaking into new markets - 42% of East of England exporters started trading in a new overseas territory, level with London and six percentage points above the national figure of 36%.
The Barometer — from the UK’s largest airports group and London Stansted owner, MAG, and the Growing Together Alliance of business groups — surveys more than 2,000 businesses through YouGov every quarter about their export performance over the past three months and their expectations for the quarter ahead.
The US was the leading market for the East of England on both measures. Almost one in five exporters (19%) reported growing sales to America, with the same proportion entering the US market for the first time.
France was the next most frequently cited market for increased sales, at 10%, followed by Australia (7%) and Spain (6%). Belgium, Canada, Germany, Poland, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates were each identified by 4% of the region’s exporters.
For new-market entry, France again ranked second, with 9% of exporters starting to trade there, followed by Australia at 4%.
Looking ahead, one in five businesses across the East of England (20%) expect to increase sales to an existing overseas market by the end of December 2026, while 11% expect to start trading in a new market.
Those figures are below the UK-wide averages of 24% and 16% respectively, showing that the region’s strong recent export performance is not yet matched by above-average expectations for the quarter ahead.
It comes after separate data produced for London Stansted by WPI Economics, revealed the East of England continues to go from strength to strength with international services trade in the region growing by 96% between 2016 and 2023. Growth was particularly strong beyond the EU, where services trade increased by 112%.
London Stansted’s Managing Director, Gareth Powell , said:
“Businesses succeed when they can connect easily with customers, suppliers and markets around the world. The latest MAG Trade Barometer highlights the strength of the East of England's international trading community, with 60% of exporters increasing sales in existing overseas markets during Q3 and 42% successfully entering new markets, making the region one of the UK's strongest performers.
"From established markets such as the US and France to emerging opportunities around the world, businesses depend on strong international connections to grow and compete. London Stansted's extensive route network and significant cargo operation help provide those vital links, supporting trade, investment and economic growth across the East of England."
Dan Thorp, Chief Executive at Cambridge Ahead, said:
“The latest figures highlight the strength of the East of England's business base, and the leading role it plays for the UK economy on the global stage.
“With the East of England reporting the highest increase in overseas sales alongside the top spot for breaking into new markets, it is clear that our region stands out for being internationally connected and active.
“International connectivity is a vital component of the Cambridge economy, which operates at the forefront of highly international and competitive innovation sectors, and these results show why investment into the Cambridge and East of England economy are so important for the UK in a global context"

O78bb8.title: NEETS review ‘a missed opportunity’
O78bb8.text:
“A missed opportunity. Milburn’s review shows a fundamental lack of understanding of how jobs are created and how emplo yers decide to invest in talent.  Minimum wage rates, employment taxes, workers’ rights and welfare handouts are the root cause of youth unemployment.  Tinkering with employment programmes and promising subsidy-driven non-jobs won’t change this.”
This is the somewhat damming verdict offered by Chris Hodson, Programme Director at Pitman Training in Essex on a major review by former minister Alan Milburn which has proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK.
Alan Milburn’s review calls for a fundamental overhaul of how Britain supports young people who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). Nearly one million young people aged 16–24 are currently in this position, around one in eight, and the report warns that the figure could rise significantly if no action is taken. Its ambition is to reduce the NEET rate to around 5% over the next decade.
Milburn argues that the problem is not simply a lack of motivation among young people, but a failure of the systems designed to support them. He proposes a new network of local Youth Opportunity Services, bringing together employment advisers, education providers, health services and other support under one roof. Every young person would receive individual guidance and a personalised plan aimed at getting them into work, education or training.
The review proposes two key guarantees: an Opportunity Guarantee , providing a route into employment, training or education, and a Support Guarantee, ensuring young people receive the practical, financial and health support needed to take advantage of those opportunities. This could include apprenticeships, college places, subsidised employment, work placements or, as a last resort, a government-funded job.
Employers would be encouraged to recruit young people through financial incentives, including grants of up to £3,000, reduced employment costs and simpler access to government support. Apprenticeships would be expanded, with a target to double participation, while schools would place greater emphasis on work readiness, practical skills and identifying pupils at risk of disengagement.
Health is another central theme. The report recommends quicker access to mental health services and support without young people having to wait for a formal diagnosis before receiving help.
However, the proposals also involve tougher expectations. A new under-25 benefits system would link financial support more closely to participation in employment, education or training. Young people who repeatedly refuse opportunities or support could face benefit reductions, although the report stresses that assistance must be available before sanctions are imposed.
Milburn estimates the reforms could help around 440,000 additional young people into work by 2036. His message is that tackling youth disengagement requires long-term investment, coordinated government action and a stronger partnership between employers, education and young people.
The central argument is that Britain must move away from a system that manages youth unemployment towards one that actively creates pathways into work, skills and independence.
The review has received a mixed reaction. Peter Richardson, Publishing Editor at BusinessTime in Essex magazine, said: “It’s an incredibly complex and difficult issue to resolve, but I’m with Chris Hoidson here What is being proposed is a bit like rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic as the vessel sinks below the surface of the water. O66d00.title: A message from Essex Wildlife Trust
O66d00.text:
A message from Justine Addison, Corporate Partnerships Manager at Essex Wildlife Trust.
This year we have again felt humbled by the support of businesses like you.
One of the greatest privileges of our work is getting to know our supporters and understanding why nature matters to them personally. Through conversations, visits and events, we hear stories about favourite places, treasured memories, family connections and the comfort and inspiration that nature provides. Those conversations continually shape our thinking and remind us why our work matters and why nature is great.
We know these are unsettled times. Many of us are feeling the pressures of change in our daily lives, whether at work, at home, or in our communities. This summer’s extreme weather brought home the reality of climate change. Here in Essex, with our long, wiggly coastline and dry weather, we are witnessing those impacts first hand. At times, the scale of the challenge can feel overwhelming.
And then there is nature.
And the outdoors.
And taking a breath.
In a rapidly changing world, nature helps us reconnect with what is important. It grounds us, restores us, and reminds us that positive change is possible.
As Essex Wildlife Trust nears to its 70 th birthday, we are reflecting not only on what has been achieved, but on what comes next. Over the decades, we have helped bring species back from decline, protected precious landscapes, restored habitats, and provided opportunities for countless people to experience and benefit from nature. For many, our reserves and green spaces have become a Natural Health Service: places where wellbeing, learning and connection grow.
This Christmas, our appeal will celebrate what makes nature great and what makes Essex special. It will tell the story of how nature enriches our lives, how our supporters have helped us make a difference over the past decades, and how together we can build on that legacy for the next 70.
Importantly, it will also launch an ambitious goal. Over the next three years, we aim to raise £1million to support the long-term protection and restoration of nature across Essex. This investment will help us care for and enhance the landscapes in our stewardship, protect vulnerable species, improve the health of our waterways, provide opportunities for people to connect with nature, and ensure that robust scientific evidence continues to guide our work. It will strengthen our ability to take practical local action, creating lasting benefits for both wildlife and people.
We believe that now is not the time to feel disheartened; it is the time to act . The appeal will last for three years as the next three years are critical – we are working towards a global goal to restore 30% of land and sea by 2030. The challenges facing nature are significant, but so too is our collective ability to make a difference. Every restored habitat, every protected species, every child inspired by the natural world begins with people who choose to invest in a better future because they understand what makes nature great.
As our Essex business community, we hope you will help us tell that story through The Great Nature Appeal and will help us write the next chapter.
Any donations made to The Great Nature Appeal between 1 st and 8 th December 2026 will be doubled by The Big Give.  Double Your donation. Double your Impact.
Thank you for your continued trust in the Essex Wildlife Trust , your generosity, and your belief in what we can achieve together.

O64b5c.title: Open letter urges place-based focus in mental health strategy
O64b5c.text:
An open letter to the government signed by close to 150 researchers, health chiefs and charities is calling for the new Mental Health Strategy for England to focus more on the places most affected by inequality.
Signatories, including the chief executives of Mind, YoungMinds, Place2Be and the Centre for Mental Health, are concerned the strategy will not fully reflect the challenges faced by coastal, rural and former industrial communities.
They warn that research, expertise and lived experience from these areas are being underrepresented in national policy discussions.
The letter to Social Care and Mental Health minister Alison McGovern MP is being coordinated by Professor Susan McPherson and Professor Victoria Bird from the Institute for Public Health and Wellbeing at the University of Essex.
Their research shows young adults in the most deprived coastal areas are three times more likely to experience undiagnosed mental distress than those in equally deprived inland areas.
Professor McPherson said: “Our research at Essex has shown that young people growing up in deprived coastal communities face particular disadvantages compared with their inland peers, highlighting that geography, as well as deprivation, can shape mental health outcomes.
“Excellent mental health research is taking place right across the country, and national policy should reflect that diversity of insight.”
The letter warns that mental health inequalities are shaped not only by individual characteristics and deprivation, but by access to local jobs, transport, housing, education, community infrastructure and other services.
It also notes that, based on publicly available affiliations, seven in ten contributors to the government’s Independent Review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism were based in London, Oxford or Cambridge.
The letter’s signatories include more than 60 professors from universities across England, many of them leading experts in health inequalities.
Professor McPherson added: “To reduce inequalities effectively, England’s mental health strategy must draw on the full breadth of expertise, evidence and lived experience across the country, rather than being disproportionately influenced by a small number of places and institutions.”
The researchers are asking government to recognise geographical inequalities in the strategy and to consider insight from a more diverse range of research leaders, local partners and people with lived experience from the areas most affected.
They are also calling for funding for local authority public health teams to invest in community-led mental health work, and for the Prevention Concordat for Better Mental Health to be revived and refreshed.
Other signatories include former Minister for Care and Support Sir Norman Lamb and leaders from universities, councils and Healthwatch organisations across England.
The team, alongside Dr Emily Murray , Director of the Centre for Coastal Communities at Essex, also set out evidence on mental health in coastal areas in a response published in the BMJ this month.
Their research found that among young people in the most deprived fifth of areas in England, those who grew up on the coast reported mental functioning scores 3.7 points lower than their inland peers.
